doc.title: Ray Blue interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 23, 2022

title: Playing for the audience; Cannonball's stage presence
summary: Blue says musicians play for listeners, and he and Rowe discuss Cannonball's welcoming way with audiences.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: I’m not sure how to phrase this question but due to your study in psychology do you think that you play to the audience or to an audience member more than other musicians?
More than? I don’t know about more than.

I guess what I’m picturing is some musicians you see them and they’re on the stage and their eyes are closed and I get the impression that they are playing totally for themselves, not that it’s — this is not a judgmental thing but then I see other musicians who seem to be a little more aware of their surroundings and who they’re playing for.

Well yeah, well I learned this too. We’re not playing really for ourselves, we’re playing for a listener and we’re communicating. Music is the language that we’re communicating with one another. There’s a connection between the audience and the artist. And I feel that it’s important to connect with that. That’s an important part of what fuels what comes out. You know? It’s important. So that’s how I view it. You know that’s how I view it. Yeah we practice a lot and these different things that we want to do as musicians and feel with the camaraderie on stage but the ultimate part is that we’re all communicating with one another to communicate with our listener.

I remember seeing Cannonball, I think I saw him live about three times. And that was a big part of what he did is that even before he played he had a welcoming delivery to the audience. He made you want to listen harder and sometimes gave you a little information about the tunes and so forth that I tried to remember as a worthwhile thing to do.

Yeah. He was like a preacher you know or a very astute professor. Yeah. What he had to say, and his voice, was one that he spoke so well. And it was also a part of his presentation, the music and all. You know? I like to — I’ve adopted some of that yeah. Sharing some information, a little storytelling, reflecting on some things that are going on on stage whether it’s between us and the audience, sure man, that’s connecting with an audience man is so important I believe. Some folks they just get up and start playing and play great every day and the audience connects with them. My thing is to connect from a personal, with some verbiage as well.
